title: RAW UNREVIEWED: Atractylis stem has a repeated spindle function in name and description
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED. In Lonitzer's complete Atractylis entry, the naming explanation says ancient women used its stem as a spindle; the later description repeats that women use the mostly bare, rough stem for a spindle. Keep the same plant part as the explicit instrument-bearer across the etymological and descriptive clauses, distinct from the plant's flowers, root, and medicinal materials. This is a source relation only, not a target gloss.

whole_source.locator: ATRACTYLIS entry, opening naming clause and subsequent description: 'caule eius antiquae mulieres pro fuso ... utebantur' and 'caulem ex magna parte nudum et asperum, quo mulieres etiam pro fuso utuntur'.
whole_source.layer: CAMENA typed edition of Lonitzer, 1551, as preserved in F_COMPLETE_ENTRIES.md; not a fully corrected diplomatic transcription.

design.content_hypothesis: One named plant part (stem) is twice assigned a non-botanical instrument role (spindle), once as the name's rationale and again in the morphology description. The repetition constrains an interpretation to preserve the same part-to-tool relation across clauses.
design.contrast: A written part-to-whole/instrument account predicts that stem owns spindle use; it does not transfer the use to the root, flower, or the plant's medicinal intake. No claim about every instance of the plant or modern practice follows.
design.smallest_next_authoring_object: If selected later, nominate one already-authorized whole target passage with independently fixed part and instrument roles; do not assign any Voynich word here.
strongest_limits: The source is a typed edition, not a corrected diplomatic or witness collation.
The entry gives no dimensions or operational details for the spindle use.
No Voynich target meaning or test is selected.
Duplicate retrieval is navigation, not a novelty verdict.
